extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students and general readers of American government and politics
extracted.subtask_description: Describes the constitutional rules, institutional arrangements, and practical consequences that shape state legislatures (apportionment, terms, sessions, limits on special laws, organization, and procedure). Useful for analyzing how legislative design affects representation and lawmaking quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: County as unit of representation / minimum one member requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The constitution of New York recognizes the county as the unit of representation by providing that each one, except Hamilton, shall have at least one member in the assembly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requirement 'plays havoc with popular representation,' producing serious malapportionment: smaller counties over-represented while populous counties are under-represented (examples: four populous counties had only twelve members whereas by population they would have had eighteen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional discrimination against cities in favor of rural districts
rubrics_metrics.description: Most state constitutions discriminate against cities in favor of rural districts (e.g., New York: no county shall have more than one-third of all the senators; 'no two counties... shall have more than one-half of all the senators').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This produces gross inequalities in representation (examples: Connecticut towns/cities allocation yielding severe mismatch between population and seats).

rubrics_metrics.name: Apportionment constitutional principles: equal, compact, contiguous
rubrics_metrics.description: State constitutions may prescribe that senate districts 'shall be as nearly equal as possible, compact in form, and consisting of contiguous territory.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also may forbid dividing counties except 'to make two or more senate districts wholly within such county' and may require assembly districts to be wholly within a senate district and forbid dividing a township or city block.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum representation and limits on county division in apportionment
rubrics_metrics.description: Provisions that 'each county, with one exception, shall have at least one member in the assembly' and that 'no county can be divided, except to make two or more senate districts wholly within such county.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These constraints can exacerbate malapportionment by guaranteeing representation to small units and restricting how districts can be drawn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apportionment done by local boards or supervisors
rubrics_metrics.description: The apportionment of assemblymen in counties entitled to two or more members may be placed 'in the hands of the board of supervisors, or the common council.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entrusting apportionment to local bodies can affect fairness and political control of districting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial review of legislative apportionment
rubrics_metrics.description: The constitution may explicitly state that 'a legislative apportionment law is subject to review by the court of appeals at the suit of any citizen.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a judicial remedy against gerrymandering; inclusion of such language gives citizens standing to challenge apportionment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cumulative / minority representation system (Illinois)
rubrics_metrics.description: Illinois law: house shall consist of three times the number of senators; three representatives elected in each senatorial district; each qualified voter may cast as many votes for one candidate as there are representatives, or distribute his votes among candidates; top three vote-getters elected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This cumulative voting system allows 'plumping' (concentrating votes) and is intended to secure minority-party representation in each district.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of cumulative voting on proportionality and gerrymander reduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Moore's study: cumulative system 'almost always secures a minority party representative in every district' and 'does away with many of the evils and gross inequalities of the gerrymander.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical example: under cumulative system in Illinois averages for Republican and Democratic representatives were substantially equal, unlike large disparities in New York and Michigan under majority systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uncertain effects of cumulative voting on party organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Conflicting opinions on whether cumulative voting increases or diminishes party organization: some say no effect; a larger number argue the party machine's influence is increased due to controlling distribution of multiple votes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cumulative voting may strengthen party control because parties must manage voters' distribution of votes ('plumping').

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguous effect of cumulative voting on legislative personnel quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Moore found 'almost insuperable obstacles' to concluding whether cumulative voting improves legislative personnel; some legislators thought it produced more representative men, others said the 'worst candidate stands the best chance' due to overdone plumping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mixed views imply trade-offs: secures minority representation but may allow less qualified individuals to win.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trend to lengthen legislative terms and debate over term length
rubrics_metrics.description: General tendency to increase length of terms: more than half the states elect senators for four years; most lower house members have two-year terms though some states have four or annual elections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments: longer terms give legislators time to learn rules and gain experience (improves effectiveness); annual elections keep them accountable ('citizens may pass upon their acts').

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualifications and representative composition of legislatures
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislators must have voter qualifications of the commonwealth; some states fix age limits. Studies show legislatures are 'fairly representative' of diverse occupational groups but many members lack prior legislative experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diversity connects legislatures with real interests and customs of people, but lack of legislative expertise means legislatures are not expert law-making bodies and quality can suffer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pay and compensation rules for legislators
rubrics_metrics.description: Many constitutions prescribe compensation; others leave determination to legislature but forbid increases during the term. Some states provide definite annual salaries, others per diem with limits tied to session length (e.g., Oklahoma: $6 per day for 60 days and $2 after).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Payment structures (salary vs per diem; limits on days) can influence legislators' incentives and session behavior; nearly all states also pay mileage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Session frequency and length constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: States vary: annual sessions are now rare; most provide biennial sessions; one state had quadrennial sessions. Constitutions sometimes fix definite periods (40–90 days) or reduce wages after a set time to limit sessions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short sessions aim to limit 'unwise legislation' by forcing focus on important matters, but may impose stress and leave insufficient time for hearings and deliberation, hampering legislative quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposal to divide legislative session into two parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Ernest Bruncken proposed abolishing the time limit and dividing session into two parts—first for introduction and committee reference, adjourn, then second for discussion and passage—prohibiting new bills in the second part except under strict control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: California adopted this idea in 1911; proposed to give time for committee work and later deliberation, addressing short-session problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six general groups of constitutional limitations on state legislatures
rubrics_metrics.description: State constitutions impose limitations falling into six groups: (1) bill of rights guarantees (jury trial, religious freedom, press and speech, habeas corpus, takings compensation); (2) provisions controlling dealings with corporations and forbidding special charters; (3) financial restrictions on incurring debt and securing publicity for financial measures; (4) framework of state government and officer terms/powers/qualifications; (5) fundamental principles re local government, public institutions, and education; (6) restrictions on power to pass special and local laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These constitutional limits shape the scope of legislative action and protect various rights and public interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between general/public laws and special/local laws
rubrics_metrics.description: General laws apply equally to all persons or classes across the state (e.g., opening of polls, shop sanitary standards); special/local laws apply to particular persons, corporations, or localities (e.g., requiring a county to build specific bridges, exempting a particular city from taxes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special/local laws are especially susceptible to corruption and favoritism; classification matters for judicial and constitutional controls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harms of unrestrained special and local legislation
rubrics_metrics.description: Unrestricted power to pass special/local laws leads to (1) localities and corporations exerting influences to secure special favors, introducing lobbying, bribery, and log-rolling; (2) the mass of special legislation obscuring important public measures and occupying legislators' time with matters of slight statewide importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such business 'appeals... to men of small calibre and also to men whose integrity is not of the best' and deters high-standard men from legislative service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional methods to limit special/local legislation
rubrics_metrics.description: Remedies include: (a) a provision that no special laws shall be passed in cases which can be covered by a general law; (b) enumerating many subjects where special legislation is forbidden (sometimes 20–30 topics); (c) classifying cities by population into groups and requiring laws to cover one or more groups rather than single municipalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enumerated prohibitions can be evaded (e.g., crafting a 'general' law that, in fact, applies only to one city). Classifications attempt to reduce evasion but have limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community approval and publication as checks on special laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Checks include giving the affected community the right to pass upon each special law (adopted in New York) and requiring publication of any proposed special law in a newspaper circulating in the locality (adopted in Vermont, New York, Oklahoma, and other states).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication enables citizens to take action before passage; community referendum gives direct local control over special measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits reduce quantity but do not eliminate need for local legislation; autonomy recommendation
rubrics_metrics.description: While various limitations have 'undoubtedly been to reduce the quantity of local and special legislation,' many such laws are necessary; where limitations are too strict, subterfuges arise. 'Certainly much could be gained by giving more autonomy to localities.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognizes trade-off between preventing corruption and enabling necessary local governance; suggests greater local autonomy as partial solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative organization: party caucus dominance
rubrics_metrics.description: In the party caucus of the majority party the speaker is chosen and general measures to be carried by the legislature are determined. The caucus keeps discipline; usually the caucus is dominated by a small and experienced group of legislative workers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caucus control steers members toward party policy and reduces independent action by legislators; critics argue against caucus discipline but comparisons to cabinet systems are made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speaker's power over committees and agenda
rubrics_metrics.description: The speaker usually appoints committees and, by judicious distribution of members, can secure predominance of his friends on important committees; he often has a committee on rules or a group of followers who 'practically determine what measure shall come up for consideration.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With many inexperienced members, the speaker can decide the fate of measures by distributing bills among committees strategically; speaker power varies but can be enormous if he has tact and capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects of inexperienced membership on legislative quality and procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Because a large number of members are wholly inexperienced, legislatures often lack small groups prepared by training and experience to undertake high-quality legislative work; many members have had no practical experience for legislative work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inexperience consumes time getting up to speed, reduces opportunity for hearings and deliberation in short sessions, increases reliance on party leaders and committees, and undermines expert lawmaking capacity.
